about: WorldScrawl prompts. Edit them in the map window: Tools > Prompt Editor. {{name}} is filled in by the game.

groups.title: Writing style
groups.flow: The prompts and lines that shape the actual prose the model writes. Each one says which process uses it (Narration, Breaking through, Expand with AI) and which step it is there. Step 1: Narration lines tell the narrator what just happened (a move, a trip, a door, breaking through, looking around) and how to describe it. Step 2: Breaking through and New room behind a door say how a new room is named and described, and Map changes says how changed places are described. Both share one line that keeps descriptions timeless (Places: timeless descriptions). Step 3: Expand with AI writes a place's description or notes in the place form. These are free to edit; prompts whose wording the game reads back stay locked in their own groups.

groups.title: Shared bases
groups.flow: Not a process of its own: the shared base for every question that asks the model to pick one option from a list (which exit to look at, what to do at a closed door, which place a window shows, which door to open or close). Step 1: the game lists the options as short text keys ("- key: meaning") and sends this system prompt with the question. The answer is matched to a key ignoring case, punctuation and extra words; if nothing matches, the question is asked once more. The shared base lines (pick.base_one, pick.base_json, pick.base_text) are the generic reply rules every system prompt ends with; each call's system prompt adds its own task line and fills the base in as {{reply}}. A saved profile that replaced a whole system prompt (without {{reply}}) keeps working as it was.

groups.title: Player intent
groups.flow: Runs on every message the player sends, before the narrator replies. Step 1: one multiple-choice question asks what the player is doing. The game builds the list of choices from the option pieces: one line per exit and per known place, plus 'breaking through', 'look', 'open/close a door' or 'a door not on the map' only when the message uses one of those kinds of words. The answer decides what happens next: an exit or place moves the party; breaking through goes to 'Breaking through'; look goes to 'Looking'; opening or closing a door goes to 'Doors'; a door not on the map tells the narrator to open it if it fits (which can lead to 'New room behind a door'); otherwise the party stays. Step 2 (only if the answer can't be read and no place name matches): a yes/no question asks whether the player is trying to travel at all. Yes means 'somewhere unlisted', no means they stay. Whatever happened is then handed to 'Narration'. Bracket commands: when the message has a known verb in brackets ("I [move] north", "[look] out the window"), step 1 is skipped. The words after the verb are matched to an exit or place by name; only if that fails, 'Bracket command: which target' asks which option they mean. If nothing fits, the game shows a note and the narrator is not called. Unknown bracket words like [OOC: ...] are ignored.

groups.title: Breaking through
groups.flow: Runs when Player intent decides the player is breaking a new opening (a hole in a wall, floor or window). Step 1: one JSON question. The game lists the nearby places (up to 3 steps away) as short keys, plus a new place where new rooms are allowed ("expandable"). The model answers with the place (an existing key, or a new name and description), the opening's name on both sides, and whether the party stays or goes through. The game checks the answer and asks once more, with the error, if it doesn't fit. An existing place just gets the linked pair of exits; a new place is made with the same "create place" edit the editor and New room behind a door use. If it still fails, nothing is changed and the narrator is told nothing gave way. Otherwise the change is saved on the player's message and, unless the answer was "stay", the party moves through. The result is handed to 'Narration'.

groups.title: Looking
groups.flow: Runs when Player intent decides the player is looking or listening. 'Look around' needs no question. Step 1: what are they looking at: around in general, one of the exits, or out of a window (only offered if a window is mentioned or the room has a view). Step 2 depends on the pick: for a closed door, ask whether they listen, peek, open it, or just look at it; for a window with no view set yet, ask which nearby place can be seen (the answer is saved so it's the same next time). The game then works out what can be seen or heard and hands it to 'Narration'.

groups.title: Doors
groups.flow: Runs when Player intent decides the player opens or closes a door. If only one door fits, no question is asked. Step 1 (only with several doors): which door. The game fills {{verb}} with "open" or "close". The game then opens or closes it (or notes it is stuck), saves that on the player's message, and hands it to 'Narration'.

groups.title: Narration
groups.flow: Not a separate model call: this is the block of world facts the game adds to the narrator's own prompt every turn, so the story matches the map. It is put together in order: Step 1 the first line; then the game's own facts, each its own entry (where the party is, the lore lines, the exits, what can be seen from here, the time, the weather; the time-of-day nudge, Narration: let the time of day show, is added only on a move, a wait, the chat's first narrated reply, or when the part of the day changed since the previous narrator reply was written; then the people-here block, built from the people label pieces); Step 2 one 'what just happened' line chosen from the result of Player intent, Breaking through, Looking or Doors (a move, a journey, breaking through, a door, a door not on the map, looking around, a look result, and so on), then any other thing that just happened (a temporary place that ran out, the place being gone, the map changing around the party, a wait, people back as they were), then on every turn without a move the stay-put line; Step 3 things passed on the way (after a move); Step 4 a nudge to mention the exits; Step 5 the last line with the rules (always the last line of the block). Alongside it, after the latest message and in this order: the arrival reminder and who is already there (move turns); a failed attempt's result; who the player's [find] brought in; who came and went; who the player's [find] did not find, and who they are. This prompt does not tell the narrator how to report changes. After the reply, a separate tracker question reads the exchange. When a saved person is in the scene, the people-here block ({{npcs_present}} and {{npc_focus}}) is added with the world facts.

groups.title: People
groups.flow: Runs when a saved person might be part of the turn. Step 1, only when the player's words do not already name one person who is here: a pick-one question asks who they are addressing or looking at (the keys are those people's ids, plus nobody). How deeply that person is described is decided from the words (a look or a talk is focused; a question about their past is deep), not a second question. The first time someone with no starting attitude is met, a separate pick-one assigns one, leaning toward indifferent. Remembering someone is its own JSON question: it reads the story since they showed up and answers with a name and one line. When the remember answer arrives, one more small JSON question (People: pick a daily pattern) chooses their daily pattern (day shift, night shift or passing through), a job (a room or an area) and a home (a room) from the listed places or off the map, and up to three favorite public spots; the game checks it, asks once more with the error if it does not fit, and otherwise falls back to passing through. The game expands the pattern into their schedule; the narrator never sees the pattern. After a story reply, the tracker question (npc.tracker) lists person, place, and wait changes from that exchange alone. The scene it reads is put together from its own pieces, each an entry: the place (npc.tracker_place), the time (npc.tracker_time), the weather (npc.tracker_weather), the people here (npc.tracker_people, one npc.tracker_person line each, with npc.tracker_unnamed for someone not known by name), the people just left behind (npc.tracker_left_person), person changes that just ran out (npc.tracker_expired), and what the game already did (npc.tracker_done). On a reply to a move it also lists the people just left behind (npc.tracker_left_behind); the tracker may say one of them came along (came_along), and the game then keeps them with the player until the next move is judged on its own. Following someone is not a tracker action (the narrator's tag still is). Appearance: each card's change is written by one compose call for its own field (People: light-touch edit or rewrite appearance fields, both with the shared People: how appearance is written), listing the active changes one line each (People: one active change in the appearance question); Looks is then summed up in its own call. NPC flagging off means it proposes no person updates; a written tag is still read. Map flagging off means it proposes no place updates.

groups.title: Map changes
groups.flow: Runs when a message is flagged as changing the map: the flag button, a [ws_flag: …] tag in a reply, or /ws-change. Step 1: given the story and an outline of the nearby map, the model answers in JSON which places changed. If none, it stops. A change only to people is not a map change, so Step 1 answers no places for it. Both steps see the flag's note through one of three pieces, picked by who raised the change: the after-reply tracker ('The change to look for'), the player, or the narrator. A place the flag names (the tracker's or the player's hint) is passed on through its own piece (Map changes: the place the note mentions). Step 2: the game sends just those places (plus neighbours and other mentions, via the pieces) and the list of map edits the editor can make; the model answers with JSON edits, or says it can't express it, or that nothing changed. How changed descriptions are written comes from the Writing style entry 'Map changes: how descriptions are written'; the edit format stays locked here. The game test-applies the edits; if they don't fit the map, Step 2 is asked once more with the retry piece explaining the error. The result becomes a review card (or is kept at once if 'keep automatically' is on). Alongside: the review card's light touch / full rewrite switch asks once more for only the change's existing texts (Map changes: rewrite the texts) and keeps every other edit; the game rejects an answer that changes anything else. Alongside: when a temporary change runs out or is turned off and a later change still in force had rewritten the same text on top of it, one call (Map changes: rebuild a text after a change ran out) writes that text again from what it was before plus the changes still in force, before the narrator reads the place; the result is kept for that set of changes, so it is not asked again. If it fails, the narrator goes ahead with the plain replay and a card offers Check again.

groups.title: New room behind a door
groups.flow: Runs when the narrator opens a door that isn't on the map yet and flags it as a discovery (from the 'door not on the map' narration). Step 1: the model gets the region and area notes, the current room, its exits, nearby rooms and the story, and answers in JSON with the new room and the door pair. If places nearby are not yet connected to this room, they are listed as short keys (the existing piece) and the model may instead answer with one of them; then only the door pair to that place is added. The new room's name and description follow the Writing style entry 'New room behind a door: how it is named and described'. The game turns that into the same 'create place' edit the editor uses and test-applies it; if it doesn't fit, Step 1 is asked once more with the retry piece. The room is added at once, as if it had always been there; its 'Map changed here' bar offers Edit, Turn off and Undo.

groups.title: Expand with AI
groups.flow: Runs when you press 'Expand with AI' under a description or notes box in the map editor. Step 1: one call with the place's region, area and connected places, which box it is (the field pieces), and your draft if the box already has text. The reply is put into the box for you to keep or change; nothing is saved until you save the form.

prompts.title: Pick one option: system prompt
prompts.description: Step 1: the system prompt for every pick-one question (Looking and Doors). The options are short text keys. {{reply}} is the shared base line pick.base_one.
prompts.locked: Shared by every pick-one question: the game reads the answer as one option key.
prompts.text: You help run a text adventure game. {{reply}}

prompts.title: Shared base: reply with one option key
prompts.description: Step 1: the shared base line for every pick-one system prompt (pick.system, intent.system). Each call adds its own task line before it.
prompts.locked: The game reads the answer as exactly one option key.
prompts.text: Reply with exactly one option key from the list and nothing else.

prompts.title: Shared base: reply with JSON
prompts.description: Step 1: the shared base line for every JSON system prompt (breaking through, map changes, new rooms). Each call adds its own task line and keys.
prompts.locked: The game parses every JSON answer; the reply must be JSON only.
prompts.text: Reply with JSON only

prompts.title: Shared base: reply with only the text
prompts.description: Step 1: the shared base line for plain-text answers (Expand with AI). The call adds its own task line before it.
prompts.locked: The game puts the whole answer into the field, so it must be the text alone.
prompts.text: Reply with only the text: no title, no quotes, no notes.

prompts.title: Breaking through: system prompt (JSON answer)
prompts.description: Step 1 of 1: the system prompt for the one breaking-through call. It sets the JSON answer: an existing place or a new one, the exit names on both sides, and whether the party goes through. {{reply}} is the shared base line pick.base_json.
prompts.locked: The game reads the JSON answer with these exact keys; changing this can break breaking through.
prompts.text:
You help run a text adventure game. The player is breaking a new opening (a hole in a wall, floor, ceiling or window). {{reply}}:
{"existing": "place key", "direction": "exit name from this side", "return_direction": "exit name from the other side", "then": "stay" or "go_through"}
When a new place is allowed, you may reply {"new": {"name": "...", "description": "..."}} instead of "existing".
direction: one of north, south, east, west, up, down, or a short new word (1-2 words) such as hole, crack, window, breach; never one already used here. return_direction: the way back from the other side (the opposite compass word, or a word like hole); never one the other place already uses. then: "stay" only if the player clearly stays on this side (only making the opening, looking or reaching through); otherwise "go_through".

prompts.title: Breaking through: where it leads and how
prompts.description: Step 1 of 1: the one breaking-through question. The game lists nearby places as keys (and offers a new place only where new rooms are allowed); the model answers in JSON.
prompts.locked: The game reads the JSON answer with these exact keys; changing this can break breaking through.

prompts.title: Breaking through: the new-place option
prompts.description: Piece of the breaking-through question, added only where new rooms are allowed. {{style}} is the Writing style entry for the new room.
prompts.locked: The game reads the JSON answer with these exact keys; changing this can break breaking through.
prompts.text: Or it can lead to a new space nobody has seen yet: then reply "new" instead of "existing". {{style}}

prompts.title: Breaking through: retry
prompts.description: Piece of the breaking-through question, only on the second try: passes the game's error back to the model.
prompts.locked: Part of the JSON retry loop: it passes the game's error back to the model.
prompts.text: Your last answer did not fit: {{error}}. Fix it.

prompts.title: Looking: at what
prompts.description: Step 1 of 2: what the player is looking at. Asks what the player is looking at or listening to. The options (key: meaning) are made by the game.
prompts.locked: The game reads the chosen option key back; changing this can break looking.

prompts.title: Looking: a closed door
prompts.description: Step 2 of 2 (a closed door): listen, peek, open or just look. Asks what the player does with a closed door. The game reads the answer as 1 to 4, in this order.
prompts.locked: The game reads the key: listen, peek, open or look.
prompts.text:
{{said}}

The {{direction}} door is closed. What does the player do with it?
- listen: only listens at it
- peek: peeks through it (a crack, keyhole or gap) without opening it
- open: opens it
- look: just looks at the closed door

Reply with just the key.

prompts.title: Looking: out a window
prompts.description: Step 2 of 2 (a window with no view yet): which nearby place can be seen. Asks which nearby place can be seen out of a window or opening.
prompts.locked: The game reads the chosen place key back; changing this can break looking.

prompts.title: Doors: which door
prompts.description: Step 1 of 1 (only when several doors fit): which door. Asks which door the player opens or closes.
prompts.locked: The game reads the chosen door key back; changing this can break doors.

prompts.title: Player intent: system prompt
prompts.description: Step 1 of 2: the system prompt for the intent question. The system prompt for the question that works out what the player is trying to do. {{reply}} is the shared base line pick.base_one.
prompts.locked: The game reads the answer as exactly one option from the list.
prompts.text: You classify player intent for a text adventure game. {{reply}}

prompts.title: Player intent: the question
prompts.description: Step 1 of 2: the question itself. {{option_lines}} is built from the option pieces below. The multiple-choice question about the player's message. The option lines come from the "Player intent: option" prompts below.

Sees only that exchange plus the live place (name and display name, full description, exits), the time of day, the known weather, each person here (Looks, Body, Outfit, facts, memories, stance and reason), on a reply to a move the people just left behind (npc.tracker_left_behind: only they can come along), and the temporary person changes the game has just ended on its own (so a story that narrates one is not reported again). prompts.text:
{{scrap}}

Player: {{said}}
Narrator: {{story}}

Report only what this exchange changed. Most exchanges change nothing about the place or people's looks.

PLACE. Report a place change only when the place itself is different in a way someone walking in tomorrow would still find: something broken, burned, built, flooded, blocked, opened up or moved, or a timed change the story says will hold for a while (smoke filling the room, a portal open for an hour). Light, weather, a fire's state, smells, sounds and who is around come and go on their own. The game already keeps them (see Time of day and Weather above), so for them place stays null. Doors under Exits are kept by the game too. A door or way that is not under Exits and actually opens is kind "discover"; coming or going by a listed exit never is.
A change is {"changed": true, "kind": "change", "note": "what changed in the place itself", "rewrite": "light", "why": "a few words"}. A discovery is {"changed": true, "kind": "discover", "note": "which door or room"}.
rewrite is "light" when one part of the place changes (splintered floorboards, a scorched wall, a smashed window) and the rest of the description still holds, and "full" when the place is remade so the old description no longer fits (an inn turned into a palace, a room burned out, a cellar flooded to the ceiling). Judge it by how much of the description the result changes, not by how many words the change takes. why names the physical change in a few story words ("the bar was smashed").

PEOPLE. Only the people listed above get items (found is the one exception). If the story changes someone who is not listed (a stranger, a background figure, the player's own character), it gets no item; it never goes to a listed person who happens to be nearby. Use a listed person's handle only when the story is about that person: by name, by what the list calls them, or plainly by "she" or "he" right after them. id is the handle in [brackets] after their name. Several items are fine. Report only what is new: the Looks, Body, Outfit, facts and memories listed above are already known, and anything under "Already done by the game" has already been applied (the Body and Outfit above are the result).
Appearance: {"id": "their-id", "action": "appearance", "intent": "what changed", "fields": "body", "lasts": "", "scope": "light", "why": "a few words"}. Appearance is something a newcomer would still see if they walked in an hour from now: an injury, a haircut or dye, new, torn or soaked clothes, a transformation. A real change as they arrive counts (they walk in soaked); being looked at or described is not a change. intent names only the change to their body or clothes ("braids tied back", "hem soaked from the river"), not how they arrived or what they did. fields is exactly one of body or outfit; a change to both is two items. The game writes Looks from Body and Outfit. If the change will pass on its own (soaked, muddy, bruised), set lasts to a duration such as "2h"; you decide, the player does not have to say that it is temporary. Leave lasts empty when it has changed for good. What someone is doing with their hands or face right now (holding, gesturing, a blush, a frown) is part of the moment, and the narrator already has it, so it gets no item: a frown is not appearance. scope is "light" when the change touches one detail (new hair color, a scar, a muddy hem) and the rest of the description still holds, and "full" when it remakes them so the old description no longer fits (turned into a gnoll, aged decades, a new set of clothes). Judge it by how much of the result changes, not by how many words the change takes: "turned into a gnoll" is short but full. why says in a few words why you picked that scope.
Fact: {"id": "their-id", "action": "fact", "text": "..."}. {{fact_rules}} Report a fact only when this exchange shows it for the first time.
Memory: {"id": "their-id", "action": "memory", "text": "..."}. {{memory_rules}} Check the exchange for memories even when looks, stance and the place did not change; nobody has to ask you to remember.
Disposition: {"id": "their-id", "action": "disposition", "value": "friendly", "reason": "why, in one short line"}, when their stance toward the player actually shifted compared to the stance and reason listed above; a passing mood is not a shift. value is hostile, unfriendly, indifferent, friendly or helpful.
Name: {"id": "their-id", "action": "name", "name": "the name"}, when someone listed as (name not yet known) has their name said in this exchange (they introduce themselves, or someone names them in front of the player).
Found: {"action": "found", "name": "their name"}, when the story brings a known person who is not listed above into this place.
{"id": "their-id", "action": "leave"}: they leave the scene.
{"id": "their-id", "action": "staying"}: they agree to stay here with the player past their usual time.
{"id": "their-id", "action": "came_along"}: someone under "Just left behind" whom this reply shows here with the player after they arrived: walking in with them, coming in behind them, or still talking with them here. Someone only seen or heard from the other room, mentioned, or saying goodbye before the player left stays where they were and gets no item.
{"id": "their-id", "action": "stay"}: they stay behind when the player moves on.

WAIT. Report a wait only when time actually passed (a long task, a rest, sleep, or a skip of at least a quarter hour), not for an ordinary exchange or a journey. A wait is {"duration": "45m", "until": "", "sleep": false, "reason": "what took the time"}. To wait until a time of day, set until instead of duration: a time of day as HH:MM on a 24-hour clock, to the minute the story gives ("17:15" for a quarter past five in the afternoon; never rounded), or one of dawn, morning, noon, dusk, evening, night, midnight. sleep is true when they sleep.

Reply with one JSON object and nothing else: {"place": null or {...}, "people": [...], "wait": null or {...}}. place, people and wait may all be set in one answer. If nothing changed and nobody gained a memory they would keep: {"place": null, "people": [], "wait": null}
